stem: A term 40+1 week newborn is delivered at your regional level 2 nursery after a shoulder dystocia and 8 minute delay to first breath. Cord arterial pH is 6.92 with base excess -18 mmol/L. At 30 minutes of age he is intubated and ventilated with adequate saturations. On assessment at 60 minutes of age he has a weak grasp reflex, absent suck, hypotonia in all four limbs and a single brief self-terminating clonic seizure. He weighs 3400 g and is on minimal ventilator settings.

data_table.Vital signs: HR 128, RR ventilated, SpO2 96 percent, temp 37.1 C
data_table.Examination: Weak grasp, absent suck, generalised hypotonia; one 20 second right arm clonic seizure at 55 minutes; anterior fontanelle soft; pupils reactive
data_table.Investigations: Cord arterial pH 6.92 (>=7.00), base excess -18 mmol/L (>=-12), lactate 12 mmol/L (<2), Apgar 2/5/6, blood glucose 3.2 mmol/L (2.6 to 5.5)

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step in his management?

options.text: Maintain normothermia at 36.8 to 37.2 C, load with phenobarbitone 20 mg/kg intravenously and arrange non-urgent transfer to the tertiary nursery for further evaluation
options.rationale: Normothermia in a term infant who meets HIE cooling criteria worsens outcome; cooling must start within 6 hours of birth and the transfer window is time critical, not routine.

options.text: Actively warm to 37.5 C, load with phenytoin 20 mg/kg intravenously and observe locally as one brief self-terminating seizure does not meet criteria for active intervention beyond warmth
options.rationale: Active warming to 37.5 C in HIE increases neuronal injury and phenytoin is not first-line for neonatal seizures in AU nurseries; the correct step is cooling and retrieval.

options.text: Begin passive cooling by turning off the overhead radiant warmer, aim for core temperature 33.5 C and arrange urgent NETS retrieval to a tertiary NICU for active whole-body cooling
options.rationale: Cord pH under 7.00, base excess more negative than -12, encephalopathy and seizures within 6 hours meet AU therapeutic hypothermia criteria; passive cooling starts locally while awaiting retrieval for active servo-controlled whole-body cooling.

options.text: Continue mechanical ventilation only, defer any temperature or antiseizure decision until formal amplitude-integrated EEG is available in 2 hours, then reassess encephalopathy grade
options.rationale: Waiting 2 hours for aEEG delays the therapeutic window; encephalopathy grade can be assessed clinically now with Sarnat and the cord gas and seizure already meet cooling criteria.

options.text: Give a 20 mL/kg normal saline bolus intravenously then 10 percent dextrose infusion at 4 mL/kg/hour, hold on cooling until circulatory status is optimised over the next 4 to 6 hours
options.rationale: A fluid bolus is not indicated without hypovolaemia and cooling should not be deferred; volume overload worsens cerebral oedema in HIE and delays a time-critical neuroprotective intervention.

explanation.summary: Term infants with cord pH under 7.00 or base excess more negative than -12 plus moderate or severe encephalopathy within 6 hours of birth qualify for therapeutic hypothermia to a core temperature of 33.5 C for 72 hours. Passive cooling starts locally while awaiting retrieval, avoiding hyperthermia which worsens injury. Seizure control uses phenobarbitone as first-line in AU nurseries. Active warming, delay, or fluid boluses are contraindicated in this window.
key_points: Cord pH under 7.00 or BE worse than -12 plus encephalopathy triggers cooling
Cooling window is 6 hours of birth; passive cooling starts locally
Target core temperature 33.5 C for 72 hours via servo control at tertiary NICU
Phenobarbitone first-line for neonatal seizures; avoid phenytoin as first-line
explanation.pearls: Sarnat staging distinguishes moderate (stupor, hypotonia, weak suck, seizures) from severe (coma, flaccid, absent brainstem reflexes) encephalopathy; both qualify for cooling but severe carries markedly worse prognosis regardless of therapy.

stem: An 8-year-old boy attends your general practice with his mother because he still wets the bed most nights. He has never had a period longer than 2 dry weeks. He passes urine normally by day, has no daytime wetting, no urgency and no straining. Bowel habit is soft daily motions. He is otherwise well, thriving on the 60th centile and doing well at school socially and academically. His father wet the bed until age 10. Urinalysis is normal.

data_table.Examination: Abdomen soft, no palpable bladder, no lower limb neurology, normal external genitalia; spine unremarkable
data_table.Investigations: Urinalysis negative for glucose, protein, leukocytes and nitrites; MSU not required

lead_in: What is the most appropriate first-line management step to offer?

options.text: Desmopressin melt 120 microgram sublingually 30 minutes before bed for a 3 month trial with fluid restriction from the evening meal until morning
options.rationale: Desmopressin is a second-line or short-term option when the family cannot commit to an alarm; it does not retrain the arousal response and relapse is common on cessation.

options.text: Oxybutynin 2.5 mg orally twice daily plus a fluid diary and reassess in 3 months with a bladder ultrasound if no improvement in wetting frequency by then
options.rationale: Anticholinergics are used for daytime overactive bladder features; this child has no daytime symptoms so a bladder-relaxant adds side effects without benefit.

options.text: Refer for urodynamic studies and renal tract ultrasound to exclude an underlying structural or neurological cause before starting any behavioural or pharmacological therapy
options.rationale: Uncomplicated monosymptomatic enuresis with normal urinalysis and no red flags does not warrant urodynamics; imaging is reserved for daytime symptoms, recurrent UTIs, or neurology signs.

options.text: Star chart and reward-based lifting overnight at midnight for 6 weeks with no other therapy, reviewing progress at the next school health check appointment
options.rationale: Lifting and simple reward alone yield lower cure rates than an alarm program; star charts are supportive but not standalone first-line at age 8 in AU pathways.

options.text: Enuresis alarm program (bell and pad) for a minimum of 8 to 12 weeks with weekly review and continuation until 14 consecutive dry nights are achieved
options.rationale: For monosymptomatic nocturnal enuresis in a motivated child aged 6 years or older, an enuresis alarm program is the AU first-line therapy with the best long-term dry rates, provided the child is motivated and parents can respond overnight.

explanation.summary: Monosymptomatic nocturnal enuresis in a child aged 6 or older with no daytime symptoms, normal urinalysis and a motivated family is first-line managed with an enuresis alarm program for at least 8 to 12 weeks. Desmopressin is a second option or short-term bridge for school camps. Anticholinergics are for overactive bladder features. Imaging and urodynamics are reserved for red flags like daytime wetting, recurrent UTI, or neurology.
key_points: Alarm therapy is first-line from age 6 with a motivated family
Desmopressin second-line or short-term for events
Oxybutynin only if daytime OAB features
No imaging or urodynamics unless daytime symptoms or red flags
explanation.pearls: Continue alarm therapy until 14 consecutive dry nights are achieved; stopping earlier predicts relapse. Overlearning by taking extra evening fluid before final dry weeks reduces relapse rates further.

stem: A 13-year-old boy weighing 84 kg presents to your emergency department with a 3-week history of intermittent right knee pain and a limp that has worsened over the past 48 hours. There is no history of trauma. On examination he keeps the right leg externally rotated at rest and has pain on internal rotation of the right hip. Passive hip flexion produces obligatory external rotation. He is otherwise systemically well.

data_table.Examination: Right leg held externally rotated; pain on internal rotation of right hip; obligatory external rotation on hip flexion; no effusion at the knee; distal neurovascular status intact
data_table.Investigations: BMI 32 kg/m2 (5th to 85th centile); no fever, no elevated CRP

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Prescribe ibuprofen 10 mg/kg orally three times daily for 5 days, gentle range of motion physiotherapy and outpatient orthopaedic review in 2 weeks if symptoms persist
options.rationale: Ambulatory NSAID therapy misses the diagnosis and permits ongoing weight bearing that can progress a stable slip to unstable, dramatically increasing avascular necrosis risk.
source_refs: RCH CPG: Slipped upper femoral epiphysis

options.text: Order urgent AP and frog-lateral pelvic X-rays, immediate strict non-weight bearing on crutches and refer urgently to the on-call orthopaedic team for probable in situ pinning
options.rationale: The obligatory external rotation on hip flexion in an overweight adolescent is classical for a slipped upper femoral epiphysis, which is a surgical emergency; strict non-weight bearing is essential to prevent further slip and avascular necrosis.
source_refs: RCH CPG: Slipped upper femoral epiphysis

options.text: Order an MRI of the knee and both hips within 48 hours with orthopaedic outpatient review to plan definitive management after imaging is available
options.rationale: MRI is not the initial modality for suspected SUFE; plain AP and frog-lateral pelvic X-rays are diagnostic and available urgently, and any delay in immobilisation risks progression.
source_refs: RCH CPG: Slipped upper femoral epiphysis

options.text: Arrange bone scan and refer to endocrinology for hypothyroidism and growth hormone screening as a metabolic underlying cause before orthopaedic intervention is planned
options.rationale: Endocrine workup for SUFE is done later in atypical cases (very young, very underweight); the immediate priority is imaging, non-weight bearing and orthopaedic pinning to prevent further slip.
source_refs: RCH CPG: Slipped upper femoral epiphysis

options.text: Discharge home with paracetamol 500 mg orally four times daily, reassurance about likely Osgood-Schlatter disease and a physiotherapy referral for quadriceps strengthening review
options.rationale: Osgood-Schlatter presents with tibial tubercle pain, not hip external rotation deformity; misattributing SUFE risks catastrophic progression and femoral head necrosis.
source_refs: RCH CPG: Slipped upper femoral epiphysis

explanation.summary: Referred knee pain in an overweight adolescent with obligatory external rotation on hip flexion is classical for a slipped upper femoral epiphysis. Diagnosis is confirmed on AP and frog-lateral pelvic X-rays. Management is immediate strict non-weight bearing and urgent orthopaedic referral for in situ percutaneous screw fixation. Delay risks further slip and avascular necrosis of the femoral head.
key_points: Adolescent hip or referred knee pain with external rotation = suspect SUFE
AP and frog-lateral pelvic X-rays are first-line imaging
Immediate strict non-weight bearing until definitive fixation
Definitive treatment is in situ percutaneous screw pinning
explanation.pearls: The contralateral hip develops SUFE in up to 40 percent of cases; unilateral SUFE under age 10 or over age 16 warrants endocrine workup for hypothyroidism, growth hormone deficiency or renal osteodystrophy.

sources.label: RCH CPG: Slipped upper femoral epiphysis

stem: A 9-month-old previously well boy presents to your emergency department with his mother, who reports 6 hours of episodes where he suddenly starts crying, draws both legs up to his chest, then settles quietly for 15 to 20 minutes before crying out again. He has vomited twice, most recently a small amount that looked greenish. His last nappy 30 minutes ago contained slimy red jelly-like material. He is now floppy between the episodes and hard to wake for feeds.

data_table.Vital signs: HR 168, RR 40, SpO2 97 percent on room air, temp 37.4 C, cap refill 3 seconds
data_table.Examination: Between episodes: pale, hypotonic, drowsy but rousable; abdomen soft with a firm sausage-shaped mass palpable in the right upper quadrant; empty right iliac fossa; nappy contents as described

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next diagnostic step?

options.text: Abdominal X-ray series (supine and erect) to identify a target sign, dilated loops or free air before proceeding to more advanced imaging or surgical consultation
options.rationale: Plain films are neither sensitive nor specific for intussusception; a normal X-ray does not exclude it and they delay definitive imaging.

options.text: Computed tomography of the abdomen and pelvis with intravenous contrast to identify a lead point and any associated bowel ischaemia before contacting the surgical team
options.rationale: CT delivers significant radiation to an infant and delays reduction; ultrasound is the AU first-line and CT is not required in typical presentations.

options.text: Trial of intramuscular ondansetron 0.15 mg/kg with 4 hours of clinical observation and repeat clinical examination before ordering any radiological investigations
options.rationale: The classical triad of colicky pain, redcurrant stool and a palpable mass is a surgical emergency; observation with antiemetics wastes the window before ischaemic bowel develops.

options.text: Urgent abdominal ultrasound performed by an experienced operator to look for a target sign and to guide the paediatric surgical team's decision on air enema reduction
options.rationale: Ultrasound has close to 100 percent sensitivity for ileocolic intussusception in experienced hands and is the AU first-line diagnostic step, allowing air enema reduction to be planned rapidly in stable children.

options.text: Take directly to theatre for laparotomy and manual reduction on clinical grounds without waiting for imaging as the classical clinical triad alone is diagnostic and time is critical here
options.rationale: Direct-to-theatre bypasses non-operative air enema reduction, which is successful in 80 to 90 percent of stable ileocolic cases and avoids anaesthesia and surgery in most.

explanation.summary: Intermittent colicky pain with knee-drawing episodes, a palpable sausage-shaped mass and redcurrant jelly stool in an infant aged 6 to 24 months is intussusception until proven otherwise. Abdominal ultrasound is the AU first-line diagnostic modality with a target or doughnut sign. In stable children, air enema reduction succeeds in 80 to 90 percent of ileocolic cases. Signs of peritonitis, perforation, or shock mandate operative reduction.
key_points: Colic + redcurrant stool + sausage-shaped mass = intussusception
Ultrasound is first-line imaging in AU
Air enema reduction succeeds in most stable cases
Operative reduction if peritonitis, perforation or shock
explanation.pearls: Recurrence after air enema reduction occurs in about 10 percent, usually within 48 hours; children are typically observed for a minimum 24 hours after successful non-operative reduction before oral trial and discharge.

stem: A term 5-week-old formula-fed infant is brought to your GP clinic by her mother because she still looks yellow. Birth weight was 3.4 kg and she now weighs 4.6 kg with normal weight gain. Her mother reports that her nappies contain pale-white stools and her wee looks dark like apple juice over the past week. She is otherwise feeding well, alert and interactive between feeds. She was born vaginally without complication and has no family history of liver disease.

data_table.Examination: Jaundice extending below the umbilicus; sclera icteric; abdomen soft with liver edge palpable 3 cm below costal margin, firm; spleen not palpable; no dysmorphism
data_table.Investigations: Total bilirubin 165 micromol/L, conjugated bilirubin 62 micromol/L (<20 micromol/L or <20 percent of total), ALT 145 U/L (<40), GGT 340 U/L (<50); FBC and film normal, blood group compatible, TFTs normal

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Urgent same-day referral to the paediatric hepatology unit for confirmation of biliary atresia by HIDA scan and liver biopsy with a view to Kasai portoenterostomy
options.rationale: Conjugated bilirubin above 20 percent of total or above 20 micromol/L in a jaundiced infant beyond 2 weeks is biliary atresia until proven otherwise; Kasai portoenterostomy before 60 days of life dramatically improves outcomes.

options.text: Reassure the mother that this is likely breast milk jaundice or delayed physiological jaundice and review in 4 weeks with a repeat serum bilirubin at that visit
options.rationale: Breast milk jaundice is unconjugated; conjugated hyperbilirubinaemia is always pathological and demands urgent workup, and the infant is formula fed.

options.text: Commence phototherapy at home and repeat serum bilirubin in 48 hours to check the trend before deciding on further evaluation or hospital-based investigations for the persistent jaundice
options.rationale: Phototherapy treats unconjugated hyperbilirubinaemia and is contraindicated in conjugated hyperbilirubinaemia where it may cause bronze-baby syndrome; the priority is diagnostic referral, not phototherapy.

options.text: Start ursodeoxycholic acid 20 mg/kg/day orally and arrange outpatient hepatology review in 4 to 6 weeks with repeat liver function testing before that appointment
options.rationale: Ursodeoxycholic acid may be adjunctive but does not treat biliary atresia; delaying referral by 4 to 6 weeks pushes the Kasai window and native liver survival falls sharply after 60 days.

options.text: Order TORCH serology and metabolic screening (urine reducing substances, plasma amino acids, galactose-1-phosphate) and review results before deciding on any referral pathway
options.rationale: Metabolic and TORCH screens are part of the workup but must not delay hepatology referral for biliary atresia; the Kasai window is the driver of urgency here.

explanation.summary: Any jaundice beyond 2 weeks of age (3 weeks if breastfed) requires a split bilirubin. Conjugated bilirubin above 20 percent of total or above 20 micromol/L is always pathological and biliary atresia is the do-not-miss diagnosis. Kasai portoenterostomy before 60 days of life offers the best chance of native liver survival, so referral is same-day to a paediatric hepatology unit. Pale stools and dark urine strongly support obstructive cholestasis.
key_points: Prolonged jaundice past 2 weeks needs a split bilirubin
Conjugated fraction above 20 percent or 20 micromol/L is pathological
Pale stools + dark urine = obstructive cholestasis pattern
Kasai before 60 days maximises native liver survival
explanation.pearls: Time to Kasai is the strongest modifiable prognostic factor: 10-year native liver survival is around 50 percent when performed before 60 days but drops to under 20 percent when performed after 90 days.

stem: A term 3.6 kg male newborn on your postnatal ward has not passed meconium 52 hours after birth. He has started vomiting greenish material with the last two feeds. His abdomen is distended and tympanic. Rectal examination causes a gush of gas and loose meconium. He was born vaginally at 39+5 weeks after an uncomplicated pregnancy. His mother had gestational diabetes controlled on diet and there is no family history of cystic fibrosis or gastrointestinal disease.

data_table.Vital signs: HR 158, RR 52, SpO2 97 percent, temp 36.9 C
data_table.Examination: Marked abdominal distension, tympanic to percussion; audible bowel sounds; per rectum: normal anus, high tone; gush of gas and loose meconium after examination; no anal pit or fistula
data_table.Investigations: Antenatal screening normal; newborn screen taken day 2, results pending; abdominal X-ray shows dilated bowel loops with paucity of gas in the rectum

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next investigation?

options.text: Sweat chloride testing on day of life 14 to exclude cystic fibrosis after ensuring adequate weight gain and hydration prior to arranging the definitive test
options.rationale: Sweat testing is used for meconium ileus workup but is age dependent and does not explain the classical explosive gush; Hirschsprung is more likely and time critical.

options.text: Trial of a warm normal saline enema 10 mL/kg with observation for spontaneous passage of meconium then reassess feeding tolerance over the next 24 to 48 hours
options.rationale: Empirical enema may temporarily decompress but risks delaying diagnosis of Hirschsprung and does not address the underlying aganglionic segment that mandates surgical planning.

options.text: Contrast enema with water-soluble contrast to identify a transition zone and refer to the paediatric surgical team for suction rectal biopsy to confirm Hirschsprung disease
options.rationale: The delayed meconium, bilious vomiting, distension and explosive gush on rectal examination are classical for Hirschsprung disease; contrast enema shows a transition zone and rectal suction biopsy is the AU diagnostic standard.

options.text: Upper gastrointestinal contrast series to evaluate for malrotation and volvulus given the bilious vomiting before considering lower gastrointestinal contrast studies or rectal biopsies
options.rationale: Malrotation is important to consider with bilious vomiting but the transition-zone pattern on abdominal X-ray and rectal exam findings point to lower obstruction; lower contrast study is the correct next step.

options.text: Anorectal manometry to test the rectosphincteric inhibitory reflex within 24 hours before proceeding to any imaging or surgical review as this is more specific for aganglionosis
options.rationale: Anorectal manometry has poor accuracy in the neonatal period due to immaturity and is not the initial diagnostic step in AU; contrast enema and rectal biopsy are standard.

explanation.summary: Failure to pass meconium beyond 48 hours with bilious vomiting, abdominal distension and an explosive gush on rectal examination is the classical presentation of Hirschsprung disease. Contrast enema identifies a transition zone from narrow aganglionic distal bowel to dilated proximal ganglionic bowel. Rectal suction biopsy confirms absence of ganglion cells and hypertrophic nerve trunks. Definitive management is a pull-through procedure once the infant is stable.
key_points: Delayed meconium past 48 hours plus bilious vomiting warrants urgent workup
Explosive gush on rectal exam is highly suggestive of Hirschsprung
Contrast enema identifies transition zone
Suction rectal biopsy is diagnostic gold standard in AU
explanation.pearls: Enterocolitis is the major early complication of untreated Hirschsprung, with fever, distension and bloody diarrhoea; it carries mortality up to 20 percent even after surgical correction and mandates aggressive resuscitation with rectal washouts, IV antibiotics and surgical review.
